name: Spring-tension distractor

card.summary: A bone-lengthening device with a built-in spring that separates the bone continuously, used in distraction osteogenesis to add length or projection to limbs or the jaw.
card.note: Surgical device; distraction procedures carry infection, nerve and bone-healing risks.

quick.overview:
A spring-tension distractor is a type of distraction osteogenesis device. Instead of being turned by hand at set times, it holds a spring that keeps pulling the two cut bone ends apart at a steady, gentle rate. The aim is new bone growing in the gap, which lengthens a limb or moves the jaw forward.

For appearance, the relevant uses are height gain through limb lengthening and facial changes through mandibular or craniofacial distraction. Published reviews of jaw distraction describe the evidence as varied, and relapse of the achieved position has been reported.
quick.how: The device is fitted during surgery after the bone is cut. Distraction normally begins after a short waiting period of about a week and continues at roughly a millimetre a day, followed by a consolidation period while the new bone hardens. Spring devices differ from manual and motorised ones in that the pulling force is continuous rather than scheduled.
quick.risks: Reported complications of distraction osteogenesis include infection (about 5 percent), bone healing in the wrong direction, hardware failure, nerve injury to the inferior alveolar nerve in jaw procedures, and tooth bud injury. Moving the bone too fast or too slowly can lead to poor bone formation. It is performed by surgeons under medical supervision.

lead: A spring-tension distractor, also called a self-acting distractor, is a device used in distraction osteogenesis, the surgical technique in which a bone is cut and its two ends are gradually separated so that new bone forms in the gap. Wikipedia describes spring-tensioned devices as ones that supply a continual separating force rather than needing scheduled manual adjustments [1].

People pursuing height or facial structure changes encounter distraction in two forms: limb lengthening, which adds centimetres to leg bones, and mandibular or craniofacial distraction, which moves the jaw or midface forward. Looksmaxxing discussions of limb lengthening and jaw surgery mention the technique, and a spring-driven design is one of the ways the separating force can be supplied [1].
Distraction itself has a long clinical history, from an 1869 proposal and a 1905 attempt to Gavriil Ilizarov's work from the 1950s, which established the rates used today [1].

chain: New bone forms in the gap
angle.text: The device is the mechanism that creates the gap in which new bone grows, so it adds length to a limb or moves the jaw forward. Results depend on the surgery and the healing period.

paras: In distraction osteogenesis, devices are grouped by how the separating force is applied. Manual devices are turned through a rod, often by a rack-and-pinion mechanism; motorised devices such as the Fitbone nail lengthen from within the bone; and spring-tensioned devices contain a spring that continually separates the bone [1].

Distraction typically has a latency phase of about seven days after the bone cut, then separation at around 1 mm per day, often split into two steps. Too fast a rate can produce fibrous tissue and nonunion, while too slow a rate can allow premature union [1].

Limb lengthening was first used for unequal leg length. Since the 1980s craniofacial distraction has been used for conditions such as hemifacial microsomia, micrognathia and craniosynostosis [1]. Unregulated cosmetic limb lengthening in India has been described, and China banned it in 2006 [1].

No studies specific to spring-tension distractors were found. For distraction osteogenesis generally, a 2016 systematic review of mandibular studies found them too weak and varied to pool and reported notable vertical relapse, and a 2018 Cochrane review of maxillary distraction in cleft patients found a single study of 47 participants [1].

Overall complication rates reported for distraction include infection about 5 percent, bone growing in the wrong direction 7 to 9 percent, hardware failure 3 to 4.5 percent, inferior alveolar nerve damage 3.5 percent in mandibular cases, and tooth bud injury 2 percent [1].

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck proposes the procedure [1].
Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical attempt [1].
Gavriil Ilizarov begins studying distraction and develops fixation devices [1].
First modern clinical report of gradual mandibular lengthening (McCarthy et al.) [1].
